## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models
  Official title       Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models
  Instructors          P. LATOUCHE, P.A. MATTEI, M.EVEN (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 30 h (lectures 30 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Theory
  Language             English: “All lectures and materials will be in English”; lectures on Zoom and recorded, in-person sessions at ENS Paris-Saclay for questions (master-mva.com)
  Assessment           Written exam: “The students will be evaluated by a written exam” (master-mva.com); Université Paris-Saclay course detail: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale”; no weights displayed
  Prerequisites        “Course on Probability” (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, statistics, computer science or physics who knows probability and linear algebra, and wants one language for latent variables, inference and generative modelling.

**Empirical first**: in the observational study simulated in ch. 11, the naive difference of means estimates a treatment effect of 1.95 when the true effect is 1.00. On the two-moons data of scikit-learn, the best Gaussian reaches an average log-likelihood of −2.73 per point, a six-layer normalizing flow −1.21 (ch. 9). Both gaps come from a model that ignores structure: hidden confounders in one case, a curved low-dimensional support in the other.

The course builds probabilistic modelling from one idea: write the joint distribution of everything, observed or hidden, as a product of simple pieces, then compute or approximate what you need from it. Graphs encode the factorisation. Inference is exact on trees (sum-product), and approximate elsewhere (MCMC, variational methods, expectation propagation). Deep generative models replace the simple pieces by neural networks and keep the same inference questions.

It shares tools with [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (Monte Carlo), [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) (diffusions) and [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html). In semester 2 it leads to [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Graphical Models: Discrete Inference and Learning](../s2-graphical-models-discrete/index.html) and [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Derive maximum-likelihood estimators for linear, logistic and Gaussian models, and compute them by closed form or Newton's method.
-   Derive and run the EM algorithm for a latent-variable model, and prove that it never decreases the likelihood.
-   Compute posterior and predictive distributions in Bayesian linear regression and Gaussian-process regression, and select hyperparameters by the evidence.
-   Read conditional independences off a directed or undirected graph (d-separation, Hammersley–Clifford).
-   Run sum-product, forward–backward and Viterbi, and learn a hidden Markov model with Baum–Welch.
-   Design and check MCMC samplers (Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs, Langevin) and variational approximations (mean field, variational EM, expectation propagation).
-   Fit a stochastic block model to a network by variational EM.
-   Train a variational auto-encoder, explain amortisation, and tighten its bound by importance weighting.
-   Compare autoregressive models, normalizing flows, GANs, energy-based models and score-based diffusion models by what they can compute.
-   Estimate an average treatment effect under ignorability with inverse-propensity weighting and a doubly robust estimator, and state what policy learning optimises.

The official prerequisite is a course on probability. The [probability and statistics refresher](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) covers it, including conditional expectation and the multivariate Gaussian. The [linear algebra and optimisation refresher](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) covers eigendecompositions, Schur complements and Newton's method. The [scientific Python refresher](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) prepares the NumPy and PyTorch code.

-   **Related courses in semester 1** — [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (risk, regression, model selection), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (Monte Carlo, MCMC), [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (Newton, duality), [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) (Langevin, diffusion), [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Foundations of Large Language Models](../s1-foundations-llms/index.html) (autoregressive models), [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html).
-   **Courses that build on it in semester 2** — [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Graphical Models: Discrete Inference and Learning](../s2-graphical-models-discrete/index.html), [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html), [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in AI](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html), [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html), [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (Gaussian processes), [Algorithms for Speech and NLP](../s2-speech-nlp/index.html) (HMMs), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) and [Biostatistics](../s2-biostatistics/index.html) (treatment effects).

The instructors listed on master-mva.com are Pierre Latouche (UCA), Pierre-Alexandre Mattei (Inria) and Mathieu Even (Inria).

### Course outline

-   **Review: probability tools** — conditional independence, Gaussian conditioning, Kullback–Leibler divergence, exponential families.
-   **Maximum likelihood, linear models and K-means** — the estimation principle and its first four instances.
-   **Latent variables** — Gaussian mixtures, the EM algorithm and its monotonicity, probabilistic PCA.
-   **Bayesian linear models, Gaussian processes and model selection** — posteriors in closed form, EM revisited, evidence, BIC.
-   **Directed and undirected graphical models** — factorisations, d-separation, Markov properties, Hammersley–Clifford.
-   **Exact inference** — variable elimination, sum-product on trees, forward–backward, Viterbi, Baum–Welch.
-   **Approximate inference I** — importance sampling, Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs and Langevin samplers.
-   **Approximate inference II** — mean field, variational EM for stochastic block models, expectation propagation.
-   **Deep latent variable models** — VAEs, reparameterisation, amortisation, importance-weighted bounds.
-   **Beyond VAEs** — autoregressive models, normalizing flows, GANs.
-   **Energy-based and score-based models** — contrastive divergence, score matching, diffusion models.
-   **Causal inference** — potential outcomes, identification, IPW and doubly robust estimators, policy learning.
-   **Research directions** — tighter bounds, missing data, diffusion theory, network models and causal machine learning (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session, even if the tools look familiar: Gaussian conditioning and the KL divergence return in every later chapter.
-   After sessions 2–4, run the code of ch. 1–3 and change one thing (initialisation, noise level, kernel length-scale) before doing the exercises.
-   After session 6, redo the HMM example of ch. 5 by hand (Exercise 5) before the approximate-inference sessions (7–8): every later algorithm generalises one of its two passes.
-   For the deep-generative sessions (8–10), the [scientific Python refresher](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) is enough; all models train on a CPU in under a minute.
-   Keep the ELBO decomposition (Key result, ch. 2) in view: EM, variational EM, VAEs and IWAE are four ways of closing the same gap.

## 0. Review: probability tools for probabilistic models {#ch0}

Every later chapter manipulates joint densities, conditions them on observations and compares two distributions. This review fixes the four tools used throughout: conditional independence, the Gaussian, the Kullback–Leibler divergence and exponential families. The [probability refresher](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) gives the background.

### 0.1 Conditional independence

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Conditional independence]{.tag} Random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent given $Z$, written $X \perp Y \mid Z$, if for all $z$ with $p(z) > 0$:
$$
p(x, y \mid z) = p(x \mid z)\, p(y \mid z).
$$

Equivalently, $p(x \mid y, z) = p(x \mid z)$ whenever $p(y, z) > 0$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Factorisation criterion]{.tag} $X \perp Y \mid Z$ if and only if there are non-negative functions $f$ and $g$ with
$$
p(x, y, z) = f(x, z)\, g(y, z).
$$

::: proof
The forward direction takes $f = p(x \mid z)$ and $g = p(y, z)$.

Conversely, integrate the factorisation over $x$, over $y$, then over both. With $\bar f(z) = \int f\,dx$ and $\bar g(z) = \int g\,dy$:
$$
p(y, z) = \bar f(z)\, g(y, z), \qquad p(x, z) = f(x, z)\, \bar g(z), \qquad p(z) = \bar f(z)\, \bar g(z).
$$

Hence $p(x, y, z)\, p(z) = p(x, z)\, p(y, z)$, which is the definition after division by $p(z)^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Graphical models (ch. 4) are nothing but a bookkeeping of such factorisations.

### 0.2 The multivariate Gaussian

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Gaussian marginals and conditionals]{.tag} Let $(x_a, x_b)$ be Gaussian with mean $(\mu_a, \mu_b)$ and covariance blocks $\Sigma_{aa}, \Sigma_{ab}, \Sigma_{bb}$, with $\Sigma_{bb}$ invertible. Then $x_a \sim \mathcal N(\mu_a, \Sigma_{aa})$, and:

::: key
[Key result — Gaussian conditioning]{.tag}
$$
x_a \mid x_b \;\sim\; \mathcal N\!\big(\mu_a + \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}(x_b - \mu_b),\;\; \Sigma_{aa} - \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}\Sigma_{ba}\big).
$$
:::

::: proof
Set $r = x_a - \mu_a - \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}(x_b - \mu_b)$.

1.  The vector $(r, x_b)$ is Gaussian, as a linear image of a Gaussian vector.
2.  Its cross-covariance vanishes:
    $$
    \mathrm{Cov}(r, x_b) = \Sigma_{ab} - \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}\Sigma_{bb} = 0 .
    $$
3.  For jointly Gaussian vectors, zero covariance means independence, so $r$ is independent of $x_b$.
4.  Its covariance is the Schur complement $\Sigma_{aa} - \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}\Sigma_{ba}$, and its mean is $0$.

Writing $x_a$ as the conditional mean plus $r$ gives the result. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A useful corollary, the **linear-Gaussian model**: if $z \sim \mathcal N(m, P)$ and $x \mid z \sim \mathcal N(Az + b, R)$, then
$$
x \sim \mathcal N(Am + b,\; R + APA^\top).
$$

The posterior of $z$ given $x$ is also Gaussian, by Proposition 0.3 applied to the pair $(z, x)$. Probabilistic PCA, Bayesian regression and Gaussian processes (ch. 2–3) are three instances.

### 0.3 The Kullback–Leibler divergence

:::: def
[Definition 0.4 — KL divergence]{.tag} For densities $q$ and $p$ with $q \ll p$:
$$
\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \int q(z) \log \frac{q(z)}{p(z)}\, dz .
$$

**Gibbs' inequality**: $\mathrm{KL}(q \| p) \ge 0$, with equality if and only if $q = p$ almost everywhere.

::: proof
The logarithm is concave, so Jensen's inequality under $q$ gives
$$
-\mathrm{KL}(q \| p) = \mathbb E_q\Big[\log \frac{p}{q}\Big] \le \log \mathbb E_q\Big[\frac{p}{q}\Big] \le \log 1 = 0.
$$

Equality in Jensen forces $p/q$ to be constant $q$-almost surely, and the constant is $1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The KL divergence is not symmetric. Minimising it in $q$ (variational inference, ch. 7) and in $p$ (maximum likelihood, ch. 1; expectation propagation, ch. 7.4) give different answers.

### 0.4 Exponential families

::: def
[Definition 0.5 — Exponential family]{.tag} A family with sufficient statistic $T$, natural parameter $\eta$ and log-partition $A$:
$$
p(x \mid \eta) = h(x) \exp\big(\eta^\top T(x) - A(\eta)\big), \qquad A(\eta) = \log \int h(x)\, e^{\eta^\top T(x)}\, dx .
$$

Bernoulli, categorical, Poisson, Gaussian, Gamma and Dirichlet laws are exponential families.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Moments from the log-partition]{.tag}
$$
\nabla A(\eta) = \mathbb E_\eta[T(X)], \qquad \nabla^2 A(\eta) = \mathrm{Cov}_\eta[T(X)] \succeq 0 .
$$

So $A$ is convex, and the log-likelihood of an i.i.d. sample is concave in $\eta$. Its stationarity condition is **moment matching**:
$$
\mathbb E_{\hat\eta}[T(X)] = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n T(x_i).
$$

::: proof
Differentiate under the integral: $\nabla A = \int T\, h\, e^{\eta^\top T}\,dx \,/\, e^{A}$, which is $\mathbb E_\eta[T]$.

Differentiating once more gives $\mathbb E[TT^\top] - \mathbb E[T]\,\mathbb E[T]^\top$. The log-likelihood is $\eta^\top \sum_i T(x_i) - nA(\eta)$ plus a constant. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Conditional independence is a factorisation of the joint density (Proposition 0.2).
-   Gaussians are closed under marginalisation, conditioning and linear maps (Proposition 0.3).
-   $\mathrm{KL}(q \| p) \ge 0$, with equality only at $q = p$.
-   In an exponential family, maximum likelihood matches expected and empirical sufficient statistics.
:::

## 1. Maximum likelihood, linear models and K-means {#ch1}

Given data and a parametric family, which parameter should we pick? Maximum likelihood answers in one line and covers regression, classification and, after a limit, clustering. This chapter states the principle, then applies it to linear regression, logistic regression and K-means.

### 1.1 Maximum likelihood

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Likelihood and maximum-likelihood estimator]{.tag} For i.i.d. observations $x_1, \dots, x_n$ from a model $\{p_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$, the log-likelihood and the MLE are
$$
\ell_n(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i), \qquad \hat\theta_n \in \arg\max_{\theta \in \Theta} \ell_n(\theta).
$$
:::

Maximising $\ell_n / n$ is minimising an empirical version of $\mathrm{KL}(p^\star \| p_\theta)$, where $p^\star$ is the data distribution. Indeed, by the law of large numbers:
$$
\frac1n \ell_n(\theta) \;\to\; \mathbb E_{p^\star}[\log p_\theta(X)] = -\mathrm{KL}(p^\star \| p_\theta) - H(p^\star).
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.2 — Consistency and asymptotic normality]{.tag} Assume the model is well specified, $p^\star = p_{\theta^\star}$, identifiable, smooth, with invertible Fisher information $I(\theta^\star)$, plus standard regularity conditions. Then $\hat\theta_n \to \theta^\star$ in probability, and:
$$
\sqrt n\, (\hat\theta_n - \theta^\star) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal N\big(0,\, I(\theta^\star)^{-1}\big), \qquad I(\theta) = -\mathbb E_\theta\big[\nabla^2 \log p_\theta(X)\big].
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* Consistency: $\ell_n / n$ converges uniformly to $-\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta^\star} \| p_\theta)$ up to a constant. That limit has a unique maximiser $\theta^\star$ by Gibbs' inequality and identifiability.

Normality: a Taylor expansion of $\nabla \ell_n(\hat\theta_n) = 0$ around $\theta^\star$ gives
$$
\sqrt n (\hat\theta_n - \theta^\star) \approx \Big(-\tfrac1n \nabla^2 \ell_n(\theta^\star)\Big)^{-1} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\nabla \ell_n(\theta^\star).
$$

The score $\nabla \ell_n(\theta^\star)/\sqrt n$ is asymptotically $\mathcal N(0, I)$ by the central limit theorem. The bracket tends to $I$ by the law of large numbers, and Slutsky's lemma concludes. Full conditions: van der Vaart (1998), chapter 5. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 1.2 Linear regression

The model is $y_i = w^\top x_i + \varepsilon_i$ with $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$ i.i.d. Stack the inputs in $X \in \mathbb R^{n \times d}$ and the outputs in $y \in \mathbb R^n$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Gaussian likelihood and least squares]{.tag}
$$
\ell_n(w, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - Xw\|^2 .
$$

If $X^\top X$ is invertible, the MLE is
$$
\hat w = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = \frac1n \|y - X\hat w\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
For any fixed $\sigma^2$, maximising in $w$ means minimising $\|y - Xw\|^2$, a convex quadratic. Its gradient $2X^\top(Xw - y)$ vanishes at the normal equations $X^\top X w = X^\top y$.

Then differentiate in $\sigma^2$: the condition $-n/(2\sigma^2) + \|y - X\hat w\|^2/(2\sigma^4) = 0$ gives $\hat\sigma^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Geometrically, $X\hat w$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the column space of $X$. Laplace noise would give least absolute deviations instead: the loss is the negative log-likelihood of the noise model.

### 1.3 Logistic regression

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Logistic regression]{.tag} For a label $y \in \{0, 1\}$ and features $x \in \mathbb R^d$:
$$
p(y = 1 \mid x; w) = \sigma(w^\top x), \qquad \sigma(t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-t}} .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — Concavity and Newton's method]{.tag} With $p_i = \sigma(w^\top x_i)$, the log-likelihood and its derivatives are
$$
\ell_n(w) = \sum_{i} \big[y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - p_i)\big], \qquad \nabla \ell_n = X^\top (y - p), \qquad \nabla^2 \ell_n = -X^\top S X,
$$
where $S = \mathrm{diag}(p_i(1 - p_i))$. So $\ell_n$ is concave.

Newton's step $w \leftarrow w + (X^\top S X)^{-1} X^\top (y - p)$ is a weighted least-squares problem: **iteratively reweighted least squares** (IRLS).

::: proof
Use $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)$. The derivative of $y \log \sigma(t) + (1-y)\log(1 - \sigma(t))$ in $t$ is $y - \sigma(t)$.

The chain rule with $t = w^\top x_i$ gives the gradient. Differentiating $-\sigma(w^\top x_i)\, x_i$ once more gives the Hessian, which is negative semi-definite since $S \succeq 0$.

Finally, the Newton step equals $(X^\top S X)^{-1} X^\top S\, u$ with working response $u = Xw + S^{-1}(y - p)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

If the two classes are linearly separable, $\ell_n$ increases along the separating direction without bound, and **no MLE exists** (Exercise 7). A Gaussian prior on $w$, that is a ridge penalty, restores existence (ch. 3).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d = 500, 3
X = np.c_[np.ones(n), rng.normal(size=(n, d - 1))]   # intercept + 2 features
w_true = np.array([-0.5, 2.0, -1.0])
y = rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w_true))

w = np.zeros(d)
for it in range(7):                       # Newton = IRLS
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w))
    grad = X.T @ (y - p)                  # gradient of the log-likelihood
    H = X.T @ (X * (p * (1 - p))[:, None])
    w = w + np.linalg.solve(H, grad)
    print(it, np.round(w, 4), f"|grad| = {np.linalg.norm(grad):.2e}")

sk = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-10, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
print("scikit-learn:", np.round(sk.coef_.ravel(), 4))
```

The gradient norm falls from 150 to $10^{-14}$ in six steps, the quadratic convergence of Newton's method. The estimate $(-0.449, 1.638, -1.103)$ agrees with scikit-learn's unpenalised fit.

### 1.4 K-means

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — K-means objective and Lloyd's algorithm]{.tag} For centres $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K$ and assignments $z_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}$:
$$
J(z, \mu) = \sum_{i=1}^n \|x_i - \mu_{z_i}\|^2 .
$$

Lloyd's algorithm alternates two steps:

1.  assign each point to its closest centre;
2.  move each centre to the mean of its points.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Lloyd's algorithm decreases $J$ and stops]{.tag} Each step does not increase $J$, and the algorithm stops after finitely many iterations at a fixed point.

::: proof
Step 1 minimises $J$ over $z$ for fixed $\mu$, term by term.

Step 2 minimises over $\mu$ for fixed $z$: the mean minimises $\sum_{i \in C_k} \|x_i - m\|^2$ over $m$, because the gradient $2\sum_{i \in C_k}(m - x_i)$ vanishes there.

So $J$ is non-increasing. Break ties in favour of the current centre: the assignment then changes only when $J$ strictly decreases. There are at most $K^n$ assignments and none can be revisited, so the algorithm stops. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The fixed point is only a local minimum: minimising $J$ exactly is NP-hard in general. In practice one uses several restarts and k-means++ seeding (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007). Ch. 2.3 shows K-means is the zero-variance limit of EM for a Gaussian mixture.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   The MLE minimises an empirical KL divergence to the data distribution; it is consistent and asymptotically efficient in regular models.
-   Gaussian noise gives least squares; Bernoulli labels give the concave logistic likelihood, solved by Newton = IRLS.
-   Separable data have no logistic MLE without a prior.
-   K-means is coordinate descent on a non-convex objective; it converges to a local minimum.
:::

## 2. Latent variables: EM, Gaussian mixtures and probabilistic PCA {#ch2}

Many models are simple only once an unobserved variable is added: the cluster of a point, the low-dimensional cause of a high-dimensional vector. The likelihood of the observed data then contains a sum or an integral over the hidden variable, and has no closed-form maximiser. The EM algorithm turns this into a sequence of complete-data problems.

### 2.1 Gaussian mixtures

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Gaussian mixture model]{.tag} A latent label $z \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ with $p(z = k) = \pi_k$, and $x \mid z = k \sim \mathcal N(\mu_k, \Sigma_k)$. The marginal density and the log-likelihood are
$$
p(x; \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\, \mathcal N(x; \mu_k, \Sigma_k), \qquad \ell_n(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\, \mathcal N(x_i; \mu_k, \Sigma_k).
$$
:::

The logarithm of a sum has no closed-form maximiser. Two pathologies deserve a warning.

-   **Unbounded likelihood**: put $\mu_k = x_1$ and let $\Sigma_k \to 0$; then $\ell_n \to +\infty$. The MLE is a local maximum away from these singularities, or one adds a small floor or a prior on $\Sigma_k$.
-   **Label switching**: permuting the components leaves $p(x; \theta)$ unchanged, so the parameter is identifiable only up to a permutation.

### 2.2 The EM algorithm

For any distribution $q$ on the latent variables, define the **evidence lower bound** (ELBO):
$$
\mathcal L(q, \theta) = \mathbb E_{q(z)}\big[\log p(x, z; \theta)\big] - \mathbb E_{q(z)}\big[\log q(z)\big].
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — ELBO decomposition]{.tag}

::: key
[Key result — the ELBO decomposition]{.tag}
$$
\log p(x; \theta) = \mathcal L(q, \theta) + \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z) \,\|\, p(z \mid x; \theta)\big).
$$
:::

So $\mathcal L(q, \theta) \le \log p(x; \theta)$, with equality if and only if $q$ is the posterior.

::: proof
Write the joint as the marginal times the posterior,
$$
\log p(x, z; \theta) = \log p(x; \theta) + \log p(z \mid x; \theta),
$$
and take the expectation under $q$:
$$
\mathcal L(q, \theta) = \log p(x; \theta) + \mathbb E_q\big[\log p(z \mid x; \theta) - \log q(z)\big] = \log p(x; \theta) - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p(\cdot \mid x; \theta)).
$$

Gibbs' inequality (Definition 0.4) gives the bound and the equality case. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

**EM** (Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977) alternates two steps from $\theta_0$:

1.  **E-step**: $q_{t+1}(z) = p(z \mid x; \theta_t)$, which closes the gap;
2.  **M-step**: maximise the expected complete log-likelihood,
    $$
    \theta_{t+1} \in \arg\max_\theta Q(\theta, \theta_t), \qquad Q(\theta, \theta_t) = \mathbb E_{p(z \mid x; \theta_t)}\big[\log p(x, z; \theta)\big].
    $$

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — EM never decreases the likelihood]{.tag} For every $t$:
$$
\log p(x; \theta_{t+1}) \;\ge\; \log p(x; \theta_t).
$$

::: proof
The entropy term of $\mathcal L$ does not depend on $\theta$, so the M-step also maximises $\mathcal L(q_{t+1}, \cdot)$. Then
$$
\log p(x; \theta_{t+1}) \;\ge\; \mathcal L(q_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}) \;\ge\; \mathcal L(q_{t+1}, \theta_t) \;=\; \log p(x; \theta_t).
$$

The first inequality is Proposition 2.2. The second is the M-step. The equality holds because $q_{t+1}$ is the posterior at $\theta_t$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Monotonicity does not give convergence to a global maximum. Under smoothness conditions, limit points are stationary points of the likelihood (Wu, 1983). In practice EM is run from several initialisations, and the best final likelihood is kept.

### 2.3 EM for Gaussian mixtures

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — EM updates for a Gaussian mixture]{.tag} The E-step computes the **responsibilities**
$$
\tau_{ik} = p(z_i = k \mid x_i; \theta_t) = \frac{\pi_k\, \mathcal N(x_i; \mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{\sum_{l} \pi_l\, \mathcal N(x_i; \mu_l, \Sigma_l)} .
$$

With $N_k = \sum_i \tau_{ik}$, the M-step is
$$
\pi_k = \frac{N_k}{n}, \qquad \mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i \tau_{ik}\, x_i, \qquad \Sigma_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i \tau_{ik}\,(x_i - \mu_k)(x_i - \mu_k)^\top .
$$

::: proof
The E-step is Bayes' rule. The function to maximise is
$$
Q = \sum_{i,k} \tau_{ik}\big[\log \pi_k + \log \mathcal N(x_i; \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\big].
$$

It separates. For $\pi$, a Lagrange multiplier for $\sum_k \pi_k = 1$ gives $\pi_k \propto N_k$.

For $(\mu_k, \Sigma_k)$, it is a weighted Gaussian log-likelihood, maximised by the weighted mean and covariance, as in the unweighted case. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal as mvn

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.r_[rng.normal([0, 0], 1.0, (200, 2)), rng.normal([4, 3], 0.7, (150, 2))]
n, K = len(X), 2
pi, mu = np.full(K, 1 / K), X[rng.choice(n, K, replace=False)]
Sigma = np.array([np.eye(2)] * K)

trace = []
for it in range(30):
    dens = np.column_stack([pi[k] * mvn.pdf(X, mu[k], Sigma[k]) for k in range(K)])
    trace.append(np.log(dens.sum(1)).sum())          # log-likelihood at current theta
    tau = dens / dens.sum(1, keepdims=True)          # E-step: responsibilities
    Nk = tau.sum(0)                                  # M-step
    pi, mu = Nk / n, (tau.T @ X) / Nk[:, None]
    for k in range(K):
        R = X - mu[k]
        Sigma[k] = (tau[:, k, None] * R).T @ R / Nk[k]

print("log-likelihood:", np.round(trace[::6], 2))
print("never decreases:", np.all(np.diff(trace) >= -1e-9))
print("weights", np.round(pi, 3), " means", np.round(mu, 2).tolist())
```

The log-likelihood rises from −3456 to −1094.66 and never decreases, as Theorem 2.3 predicts. The estimated weights are $(0.57, 0.43)$ for true proportions $(0.57, 0.43)$, and the means are close to $(0, 0)$ and $(4, 3)$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — K-means as a limit of EM]{.tag} Fix $\Sigma_k = \varepsilon I$ and $\pi_k = 1/K$, and run EM on the means only. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the responsibilities become hard assignments to the closest mean, and EM becomes Lloyd's algorithm.

::: proof
The responsibilities are a softmax:
$$
\tau_{ik} = \frac{\exp(-\|x_i - \mu_k\|^2 / 2\varepsilon)}{\sum_l \exp(-\|x_i - \mu_l\|^2 / 2\varepsilon)} .
$$

As $\varepsilon \to 0$, this tends to $1$ for the closest centre and $0$ elsewhere, assuming no ties. The mean update becomes the cluster mean. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 2.4 Probabilistic PCA

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Probabilistic PCA (Tipping and Bishop, 1999)]{.tag} With $q < d$:
$$
z \sim \mathcal N(0, I_q), \qquad x \mid z \sim \mathcal N(Wz + \mu,\; \sigma^2 I_d).
$$

By the linear-Gaussian model of ch. 0.2, the marginal is $x \sim \mathcal N(\mu, C)$ with $C = WW^\top + \sigma^2 I_d$.

With $M = W^\top W + \sigma^2 I_q$, the posterior of the latent variable is
$$
z \mid x \sim \mathcal N\big(M^{-1} W^\top (x - \mu),\; \sigma^2 M^{-1}\big).
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — Maximum-likelihood PPCA]{.tag} Let $S$ be the empirical covariance, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d$ and eigenvectors $U = (u_1, \dots, u_d)$. The MLE is $\hat\mu = \bar x$, and, for any rotation $R \in O(q)$:
$$
\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{d - q}\sum_{j = q+1}^d \lambda_j, \qquad \hat W = U_q\,(\Lambda_q - \hat\sigma^2 I)^{1/2} R .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* Up to constants, the log-likelihood is
$$
\ell_n = -\frac n2 \big[\log|C| + \mathrm{tr}(C^{-1}S)\big].
$$

1.  The gradient in $W$ vanishes when $S C^{-1} W = W$.
2.  The identity $C^{-1}W = W M^{-1}$ turns this into $SW = W M$.
3.  Take the singular value decomposition $W = L D V^\top$ and substitute. Each column $l_j$ with $d_j > 0$ satisfies
    $$
    S\, l_j = (\sigma^2 + d_j^2)\, l_j .
    $$
    So $l_j$ is an eigenvector of $S$, and $d_j^2 = \lambda_j - \sigma^2$.
4.  Substituting back, the optimal $\sigma^2$ is the mean of the discarded eigenvalues.
5.  Comparing the values of $\ell_n$, the maximum keeps the $q$ largest eigenvalues.

Details: Tipping and Bishop (1999), appendix A. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

As $\sigma^2 \to 0$, the posterior mean projects $x$ onto the principal subspace: classical PCA is the noiseless limit. EM for PPCA costs $O(ndq)$ per iteration instead of a full eigendecomposition, and handles missing coordinates naturally.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n, d, q = 2000, 5, 2
W_true = rng.normal(size=(d, q))
X = rng.normal(size=(n, q)) @ W_true.T + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(n, d)) + 1.0

S = np.cov(X, rowvar=False, bias=True)          # ML covariance (divides by n)
lam, U = np.linalg.eigh(S)
lam, U = lam[::-1], U[:, ::-1]                   # decreasing eigenvalues
sigma2 = lam[q:].mean()                          # Theorem 2.7: discarded variance
W = U[:, :q] * np.sqrt(lam[:q] - sigma2)         # rotation R = I

C = W @ W.T + sigma2 * np.eye(d)
ll = -0.5 * n * (d * np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.linalg.slogdet(C)[1]
                 + np.trace(np.linalg.solve(C, S)))
pca = PCA(n_components=q).fit(X)
print(f"sigma2 = {sigma2:.4f} (true 0.09); scikit-learn: {pca.noise_variance_:.4f}")
print(f"average log-likelihood {ll / n:.4f}; scikit-learn PCA.score: {pca.score(X):.4f}")
```

The estimate $\hat\sigma^2 = 0.0899$ recovers the true noise variance $0.09$. The average log-likelihood, $-5.1007$, equals scikit-learn's `PCA.score`, which implements the PPCA likelihood.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   The log-likelihood is the ELBO plus a KL gap: EM closes the gap (E-step), then raises the bound (M-step).
-   EM never decreases the likelihood, but it can stop at a local maximum or a saddle.
-   For Gaussian mixtures, EM is soft K-means with covariances; K-means is its zero-variance limit.
-   PPCA has a closed-form MLE given by the top eigenvectors; PCA is its noiseless limit.
:::

## 3. Bayesian linear models, Gaussian processes and model selection {#ch3}

Maximum likelihood returns one parameter and no uncertainty, and it always prefers the most complex model. A prior on the parameters gives a posterior, a predictive distribution with error bars and a marginal likelihood to compare models. Gaussian priors keep every computation in closed form.

### 3.1 Bayesian linear regression

The model takes a prior $w \sim \mathcal N(0, \alpha^{-1} I_d)$ and a likelihood $y \mid w \sim \mathcal N(Xw, \beta^{-1} I_n)$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are precisions.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.1 — Posterior and predictive distributions]{.tag} The posterior is $w \mid y \sim \mathcal N(m_N, S_N)$ with
$$
S_N = (\alpha I + \beta X^\top X)^{-1}, \qquad m_N = \beta\, S_N X^\top y .
$$

At a new input $x_\ast$, the predictive distribution is
$$
y_\ast \mid y \sim \mathcal N\big(m_N^\top x_\ast,\;\; \beta^{-1} + x_\ast^\top S_N\, x_\ast\big).
$$

::: proof
The log-posterior is, up to a constant,
$$
-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|w\|^2 - \frac{\beta}{2}\|y - Xw\|^2 = -\frac12 w^\top(\alpha I + \beta X^\top X) w + \beta\, w^\top X^\top y + \text{const}.
$$

This quadratic form identifies the Gaussian with precision $S_N^{-1}$ and mean $S_N\, \beta X^\top y$.

For the prediction, $y_\ast = w^\top x_\ast + \varepsilon_\ast$, where $\varepsilon_\ast$ is independent of $w$ given the data. Means and variances add. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The posterior mean is the **ridge** estimator with penalty $\lambda = \alpha / \beta$, which is also the MAP estimate. The predictive variance has two terms: the noise $\beta^{-1}$, and the parameter uncertainty $x_\ast^\top S_N x_\ast$, which shrinks as data accumulate.

::: ex
[Example 3.2 — A two-point posterior]{.tag} Take one feature, data $x = (1, 2)$, $y = (1, 3)$ and $\alpha = \beta = 1$.

-   $X^\top X = 5$ and $X^\top y = 7$, so $S_N = 1/6$ and $m_N = 7/6 \approx 1.17$.
-   Least squares would give $7/5 = 1.4$: the prior shrinks the slope towards $0$.
-   At $x_\ast = 3$, the predictive mean is $3.5$ and the predictive variance is $1 + 9/6 = 2.5$.

$$
y_\ast \mid y \sim \mathcal N(3.5,\; 2.5).
$$
:::

### 3.2 Gaussian processes

Replace $x$ by features $\phi(x)$. Under the prior of ch. 3.1, the function $f(x) = w^\top \phi(x)$ has Gaussian finite-dimensional marginals with covariance $\alpha^{-1}\phi(x)^\top \phi(x')$. A Gaussian process specifies this covariance directly, through a kernel.

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Gaussian process]{.tag} A random function $f$ is a Gaussian process $\mathcal{GP}(m, k)$ if every finite vector $(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n))$ is Gaussian with mean $(m(x_i))_i$ and covariance $(k(x_i, x_j))_{ij}$.

The kernel must be positive semi-definite. A standard choice is the squared-exponential kernel:
$$
k(x, x') = s^2 \exp\Big(-\frac{\|x - x'\|^2}{2\ell^2}\Big).
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Gaussian-process regression]{.tag} Observe $y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i$ with $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k)$ and $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$. Write $K = (k(x_i, x_j))_{ij}$ and $k_\ast = (k(x_i, x_\ast))_i$. Then $f(x_\ast) \mid y$ is Gaussian with
$$
\mu_\ast = k_\ast^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y, \qquad \sigma^2_\ast = k(x_\ast, x_\ast) - k_\ast^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} k_\ast .
$$

The log marginal likelihood (the **evidence**) is
$$
\log p(y) = -\frac12 y^\top (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y - \frac12 \log |K + \sigma^2 I| - \frac n2 \log 2\pi .
$$

::: proof
The pair $(y, f(x_\ast))$ is Gaussian, with $\mathrm{Cov}(y) = K + \sigma^2 I$ and cross-covariance $k_\ast$. Apply Proposition 0.3. The evidence is the density of $y \sim \mathcal N(0, K + \sigma^2 I)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The evidence balances a data-fit term against a complexity term, the log-determinant. Hyperparameters such as $\ell$ are chosen by maximising it (type-II maximum likelihood). Exact inference costs $O(n^3)$ through a Cholesky factorisation.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x = np.sort(rng.uniform(-3, 3, 20))
y = np.sin(2 * x) + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=20)
xs = np.linspace(-3, 3, 7)

def k(a, b, ell):                       # squared-exponential kernel
    return np.exp(-0.5 * (a[:, None] - b[None, :]) ** 2 / ell ** 2)

def gp(ell, s2=0.01):
    Ky = k(x, x, ell) + s2 * np.eye(len(x))
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(Ky)
    alpha = np.linalg.solve(L.T, np.linalg.solve(L, y))
    mean = k(xs, x, ell) @ alpha
    V = np.linalg.solve(L, k(x, xs, ell))
    var = 1.0 - (V ** 2).sum(0)          # k(x*, x*) = 1
    logev = -0.5 * y @ alpha - np.log(np.diag(L)).sum() - 0.5 * len(x) * np.log(2 * np.pi)
    return mean, var, logev

for ell in [0.1, 0.5, 2.0]:
    m, v, le = gp(ell)
    print(f"ell = {ell:3.1f}   log evidence = {le:8.2f}   max posterior sd = {np.sqrt(v.max()):.2f}")
m, v, _ = gp(0.5)
print("x      ", xs.round(1))
print("mean   ", m.round(2))
print("sd     ", np.sqrt(v).round(2))
print("sin(2x)", np.sin(2 * xs).round(2))
```

The log evidence is −17.7 for a length-scale of 0.1 (too flexible), −6.0 for 0.5 and −97.6 for 2 (too rigid). With length-scale 0.5, the posterior standard deviation is between 0.08 and 0.22 at the test inputs from −2 to 2, where the data lie. It reaches 0.48 at $x = 3$ and 0.66 at $x = -3$, beyond the extreme training inputs −2.49 and 2.74.

### 3.3 EM revisited

The proof of Theorem 2.3 used only the function $\mathcal L(q, \theta)$. Neal and Hinton (1998) call $\mathcal L$ the (negative) **free energy** and read EM as coordinate ascent on it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — EM as coordinate ascent on the free energy]{.tag} The E-step maximises $\mathcal L(\cdot, \theta_t)$ over all distributions $q$, and the M-step maximises $\mathcal L(q_{t+1}, \cdot)$ over $\theta$.

Moreover, assume the posterior $p(z \mid x; \theta)$ depends continuously on $\theta$. If $(q^\star, \theta^\star)$ is a local maximum of $\mathcal L$, then $\theta^\star$ is a local maximum of $\log p(x; \theta)$.

::: proof
The first claim is Proposition 2.2: for fixed $\theta$, $\mathcal L$ is maximal when the KL term is zero.

For the second, write $q_\theta$ for the posterior at $\theta$.

1.  $\mathcal L(\cdot, \theta^\star)$ is concave in $q$, so its local maximum $q^\star$ is the global one: $q^\star = q_{\theta^\star}$.
2.  For $\theta$ near $\theta^\star$, continuity puts $(q_\theta, \theta)$ near $(q^\star, \theta^\star)$.
3.  The bound is tight at both pairs, and $(q^\star, \theta^\star)$ is a local maximum of $\mathcal L$, so
    $$
    \log p(x; \theta) = \mathcal L(q_\theta, \theta) \;\le\; \mathcal L(q^\star, \theta^\star) = \log p(x; \theta^\star).
    $$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This view justifies several variants, since any step that increases $\mathcal L$ keeps the monotonicity.

-   **Generalised EM**: the M-step only increases $\mathcal L$, for example by one gradient step.
-   **Incremental EM**: the E-step updates the posterior of one data point at a time.
-   **MAP-EM**: adding $\log p(\theta)$ to $\mathcal L$ gives the posterior mode instead of the MLE.
-   **Variational EM**: $q$ is restricted to a tractable family, and the bound is no longer tight (ch. 7.2).

**EM for the evidence of Bayesian regression.** In ch. 3.1, treat $w$ as the latent variable and $\theta = (\alpha, \beta)$ as the parameter. The E-step is Proposition 3.1, $q(w) = \mathcal N(m_N, S_N)$. With $d$ weights and $n$ observations, maximising the expected complete log-likelihood gives
$$
\alpha \leftarrow \frac{d}{\|m_N\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}\, S_N}, \qquad \beta \leftarrow \frac{n}{\|y - Xm_N\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}(X S_N X^\top)} .
$$

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal as mvn
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

# EM for the hyperparameters (alpha, beta) of Bayesian linear regression
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
N, M = 30, 10
x = rng.uniform(0, 1, N)
y = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x) + 0.2 * rng.normal(size=N)        # true beta = 25
Phi = np.vander(x, M, increasing=True)                       # degree-9 polynomial
alpha, beta = 1.0, 1.0
for it in range(200):
    S = np.linalg.inv(alpha * np.eye(M) + beta * Phi.T @ Phi)  # E-step: q(w) = N(m, S)
    m = beta * S @ Phi.T @ y
    alpha = M / (m @ m + np.trace(S))                          # M-step
    beta = N / (np.sum((y - Phi @ m) ** 2) + np.trace(Phi @ S @ Phi.T))
    if it in (0, 9, 199):
        C = Phi @ Phi.T / alpha + np.eye(N) / beta
        print(f"iter {it + 1:3d}: alpha {alpha:7.3f}  beta {beta:6.2f}"
              f"  log evidence {mvn.logpdf(y, np.zeros(N), C):7.3f}")

# Model selection: BIC for the number of mixture components
X = np.r_[rng.normal(0, 1, (150, 2)), rng.normal([5, 0], 1, (150, 2)), rng.normal([2, 4], 1, (150, 2))]
bic = [GaussianMixture(K, n_init=3, random_state=0).fit(X).bic(X) for K in range(1, 7)]
print("BIC for K = 1..6:", np.round(bic, 1), "-> K =", 1 + int(np.argmin(bic)))
```

The log evidence climbs from $-19.7$ to $-8.7$. The noise precision reaches $\beta \approx 35$, of the order of the true value 25 (the flexible fit absorbs part of the noise), and $\alpha$ falls to 0.01. A degree-9 polynomial fitted to 30 noisy points is thus regularised without any validation set.

### 3.4 Model selection

Comparing models $\mathcal M_1, \mathcal M_2, \dots$ by their maximised likelihood always favours the largest. Three corrections are standard.

-   **Evidence**: the Bayesian answer compares the marginal likelihoods $p(\mathcal D \mid \mathcal M)$, which penalise unused flexibility automatically (ch. 3.2–3.3).

    $$
    p(\mathcal D \mid \mathcal M) = \int p(\mathcal D \mid \theta, \mathcal M)\, p(\theta \mid \mathcal M)\, d\theta .
    $$
-   **BIC**: a large-sample approximation of the log evidence (Schwarz, 1978).
-   **AIC and cross-validation**: estimates of the expected predictive log-likelihood (Akaike, 1974), and its direct empirical estimate.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Laplace approximation and BIC]{.tag} For a regular model with $k$ free parameters and $n$ i.i.d. observations:
$$
\log p(\mathcal D \mid \mathcal M) = \ell_n(\hat\theta) - \frac{k}{2}\log n + O_P(1), \qquad \mathrm{BIC} = -2\,\ell_n(\hat\theta) + k \log n .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* Expand $\ell_n$ to second order around $\hat\theta$, where its gradient vanishes, with $H_n = -\nabla^2 \ell_n(\hat\theta)$. Laplace's method gives
$$
\int e^{\ell_n(\theta)} p(\theta)\, d\theta \approx e^{\ell_n(\hat\theta)}\, p(\hat\theta)\, (2\pi)^{k/2} |H_n|^{-1/2}.
$$

Since $H_n \approx n\, I(\hat\theta)$, we have $\log |H_n| = k \log n + O_P(1)$. The other terms are $O_P(1)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

AIC replaces $k \log n$ by $2k$. It targets prediction, while BIC is consistent for selecting the true model in a finite list. In the code above, BIC over Gaussian mixtures with $K = 1, \dots, 6$ components is minimal at $K = 3$, the true number. A full-covariance mixture in dimension 2 has $6K - 1$ free parameters.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Gaussian prior plus Gaussian likelihood gives a Gaussian posterior; its mean is ridge regression.
-   A Gaussian process is Bayesian regression with a kernel; prediction is Gaussian conditioning, at cost $O(n^3)$.
-   EM is coordinate ascent on the free energy, which justifies partial, incremental, MAP and variational variants.
-   Evidence, BIC, AIC and cross-validation all penalise complexity; BIC is the Laplace approximation of the evidence.
:::

## 4. Directed and undirected graphical models {#ch4}

A joint distribution of $n$ binary variables has $2^n - 1$ free parameters, far too many to store or learn. Graphical models restrict the joint to a product of local factors, and the graph tells which conditional independences follow. Directed graphs encode generative stories; undirected graphs encode symmetric interactions.

### 4.1 Directed graphical models

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Directed graphical model (Bayesian network)]{.tag} Let $G$ be a directed acyclic graph (DAG) on $\{1, \dots, n\}$, and write $\pi_i$ for the parents of node $i$. A distribution **factorises** according to $G$ if
$$
p(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i \mid x_{\pi_i}).
$$
:::

For binary variables the factorisation needs $\sum_i 2^{|\pi_i|}$ parameters instead of $2^n - 1$. The models of ch. 1–3 are all directed graphical models.

-   **Naive Bayes**: a class $y$ with arrows to each feature $x_j$, so the features are independent given the class.
-   **Gaussian mixture**: $z_i \to x_i$, repeated over $i$; a *plate* drawn around the pair stands for the $n$ copies.
-   **Bayesian regression**: $w \to y_i \leftarrow x_i$, with the plate over $i$.
-   **Hidden Markov model** (ch. 5.3): a chain $z_1 \to z_2 \to \dots \to z_T$, with an arrow $z_t \to x_t$ at each step.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Local Markov property]{.tag} If $p$ factorises according to $G$, each variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents.

::: proof
A child of a descendant of $i$ is again a descendant, so some topological order puts all the descendants of $i$ last. Sum the factorisation over them, starting from the last node: each summed factor $p(x_j \mid x_{\pi_j})$ integrates to $1$.

What remains is the product of the factors of $i$ and of its non-descendants. No non-descendant has $i$ as a parent, so $x_i$ appears only in $p(x_i \mid x_{\pi_i})$. Proposition 0.2 then gives the independence of $x_i$ and its non-descendants given $x_{\pi_i}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 4.2 d-separation and explaining away

Three structures on three nodes $a, c, b$ contain all the cases.

-   **Chain** $a \to c \to b$: the joint is $p(a)\,p(c \mid a)\,p(b \mid c)$, of the form $f(a, c)\, g(b, c)$. So $a \perp b \mid c$ by Proposition 0.2.
-   **Fork** $a \leftarrow c \to b$: the joint $p(c)\,p(a \mid c)\,p(b \mid c)$ has the same form, so again $a \perp b \mid c$.
-   **Collider** $a \to c \leftarrow b$: summing over $c$ gives $p(a, b) = p(a)\, p(b)$, so $a \perp b$. Conditioning on $c$ (or on a descendant of $c$) creates a dependence.

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — d-separation]{.tag} A path between two nodes is **blocked** by a set $C$ if it contains a node $m$ such that:

-   the arrows meet head-to-tail or tail-to-tail at $m$, and $m \in C$; or
-   the arrows meet head-to-head at $m$ (a collider), and neither $m$ nor any descendant of $m$ is in $C$.

Sets $A$ and $B$ are **d-separated** by $C$ if every path from $A$ to $B$ is blocked by $C$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Global Markov property of DAGs]{.tag} If $p$ factorises according to $G$ and $C$ d-separates $A$ from $B$, then:
$$
x_A \perp x_B \mid x_C .
$$

Conversely, when $C$ does not d-separate $A$ from $B$, some distribution factorising according to $G$ violates this independence.

::: proof
*Sketch.* The first part follows from Proposition 4.11 below: d-separation is equivalent to ordinary separation in a moralised ancestral graph, where Proposition 4.7 applies. Completeness is due to Geiger, Verma and Pearl (1990); see Koller and Friedman (2009), chapter 3. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.5 — Explaining away]{.tag} A burglary $B$ and an earthquake $E$, independent with $P(B = 1) = 0.01$ and $P(E = 1) = 0.02$, can both trigger an alarm $A$: a collider $B \to A \leftarrow E$. Take
$$
P(A = 1 \mid B, E) = 0.001,\ 0.94,\ 0.29,\ 0.95 \quad \text{for } (B, E) = (0,0),\ (1,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,1).
$$

-   Hearing the alarm raises the probability of a burglary from 0.01 to $P(B = 1 \mid A = 1) \approx 0.583$.
-   Learning that an earthquake happened brings it back down: $P(B = 1 \mid A = 1, E = 1) \approx 0.032$.

$$
P(B = 1 \mid A = 1) \approx 0.583, \qquad P(B = 1 \mid A = 1, E = 1) \approx 0.032 .
$$

The two causes were independent; given their common effect, they compete.
:::

### 4.3 Undirected graphical models

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Undirected graphical model (Markov random field)]{.tag} Let $G$ be an undirected graph and $\mathcal C$ its cliques. A distribution **factorises** over $G$ if, for non-negative potentials $\psi_C$:
$$
p(x) = \frac{1}{Z} \prod_{C \in \mathcal C} \psi_C(x_C), \qquad Z = \sum_x \prod_{C \in \mathcal C} \psi_C(x_C).
$$

When all potentials are positive, $p(x) = \exp(-E(x))/Z$ with **energy** $E(x) = -\sum_C \log \psi_C(x_C)$: a Gibbs distribution.
:::

The normalising constant $Z$, the **partition function**, is a sum over exponentially many states. It is the main computational obstacle of undirected models, and it returns with energy-based models in ch. 10.

Three Markov properties can hold with respect to $G$, from weakest to strongest:

-   **pairwise**: two non-adjacent variables are independent given all the others;
-   **local**: a variable is independent of the rest given its neighbours;
-   **global**: $x_A \perp x_B \mid x_S$ whenever $S$ separates $A$ from $B$ in $G$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Factorisation implies the global Markov property]{.tag} If $p$ factorises over $G$ and $S$ separates $A$ from $B$, then $x_A \perp x_B \mid x_S$.

::: proof
Let $\tilde A$ be the union of the connected components of $G \setminus S$ that meet $A$, and $\tilde B$ the rest of $V \setminus S$, which contains $B$.

No edge joins $\tilde A$ to $\tilde B$. So every clique lies in $\tilde A \cup S$ or in $\tilde B \cup S$, and grouping the potentials gives
$$
p(x) = f(x_{\tilde A}, x_S)\; g(x_{\tilde B}, x_S).
$$

Proposition 0.2 gives $x_{\tilde A} \perp x_{\tilde B} \mid x_S$, and the claim follows by marginalisation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 4.4 Hammersley–Clifford, Ising and Gaussian graphical models

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.8 — Hammersley–Clifford]{.tag} Let $p(x) > 0$ for all $x$. Then $p$ satisfies the pairwise Markov property with respect to $G$ if and only if it factorises over the cliques of $G$.

::: proof
*Sketch.* The reverse direction is Proposition 4.7. For the direct one, fix a reference state $x^\ast$. For each set $A$, let $x^A$ agree with $x$ on $A$ and with $x^\ast$ elsewhere, and define by Möbius inversion
$$
\phi_A(x) = \sum_{B \subseteq A} (-1)^{|A \setminus B|} \log p(x^B), \qquad \text{so that} \qquad \log p(x) = \sum_{A} \phi_A(x).
$$

If $A$ contains two non-adjacent nodes $i$ and $j$, group the terms of $\phi_A$ in fours, according to whether $B$ contains each of the two nodes. Each group is a difference of differences of $\log p$.

The pairwise property makes it vanish, because $\log p$ is a sum of a term without $x_i$ and a term without $x_j$.

So $\phi_A = 0$ unless $A$ is a clique (Besag, 1974; Lauritzen, 1996, chapter 3). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Positivity is needed: there are distributions with zeros that satisfy the Markov properties without factorising.

**The Ising model.** For spins $x \in \{-1, +1\}^n$ on a graph:
$$
p(x) = \frac1Z \exp\Big(\sum_i h_i x_i + \sum_{(i,j) \in E} J_{ij}\, x_i x_j\Big).
$$

It is the prototype of a pairwise Markov random field. Computing its $Z$ on a general graph is #P-hard, which motivates the samplers of ch. 6 (Exercise 10).

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.9 — Gaussian graphical models]{.tag} Let $x \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \Theta^{-1})$ with precision matrix $\Theta$. Then for $i \ne j$:
$$
x_i \perp x_j \mid x_{\text{rest}} \iff \Theta_{ij} = 0 .
$$

::: proof
The density is proportional to $\exp\big(-\frac12 (x - \mu)^\top \Theta (x - \mu)\big)$. The only term coupling $x_i$ and $x_j$ is $-\Theta_{ij}(x_i - \mu_i)(x_j - \mu_j)$. If $\Theta_{ij} = 0$, the density factorises as $f(x_i, x_{\text{rest}})\, g(x_j, x_{\text{rest}})$, and Proposition 0.2 applies.

Conversely, the conditional covariance of $(x_i, x_j)$ given the rest is the inverse of the $2 \times 2$ block of $\Theta$ on $\{i, j\}$, by Proposition 0.3 and the block-inverse formula. Its off-diagonal entry is zero only if $\Theta_{ij} = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

So the graph of a Gaussian model is read off the zeros of its precision matrix. Estimating a sparse precision matrix with an $\ell_1$ penalty is the graphical lasso (Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani, 2008).

### 4.5 From directed to undirected: moralisation

::: def
[Definition 4.10 — Moral graph]{.tag} The moral graph of a DAG is obtained by joining (“marrying”) every pair of parents of a common child, then dropping the directions.
:::

Each factor $p(x_i \mid x_{\pi_i})$ is a potential on the set $\{i\} \cup \pi_i$, which is a clique of the moral graph. So a directed factorisation is a Gibbs factorisation on the moral graph, with $Z = 1$. The converse fails: moralisation hides the marginal independence of the two parents of a collider.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.11 — d-separation by moralisation]{.tag} Let $H$ be the moral graph of the smallest ancestral set containing $A \cup B \cup C$.

Then d-separation of $A$ and $B$ by $C$ in $G$ is equivalent to separation by $C$ in $H$.

::: proof
*Sketch.* Summing out the nodes outside an ancestral set leaves a directed factorisation on that set, as in the proof of Proposition 4.2. Moralising it gives a Gibbs factorisation, and Proposition 4.7 applies.

The equivalence of the two separation criteria is a combinatorial argument on paths (Lauritzen, 1996, chapter 3). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   A DAG factorises the joint into conditionals of each node given its parents; the separation criterion is d-separation.
-   Colliders are special: conditioning on a common effect couples its causes (explaining away).
-   An undirected model factorises into clique potentials divided by the partition function $Z$.
-   For positive distributions, pairwise Markov and clique factorisation are equivalent (Hammersley–Clifford).
-   In a Gaussian model, missing edges are the zeros of the precision matrix.
:::

## 5. Exact inference: the sum-product algorithm and hidden Markov models {#ch5}

Once a model is written, every question about it is a sum: a marginal, a conditional given evidence, the partition function. Done naively, these sums have exponentially many terms. On trees, the distributive law reduces them to messages passed along the edges, at linear cost.

### 5.1 Variable elimination and factor graphs

Take a chain $x_1 - x_2 - \dots - x_n$ with $K$ states each and pairwise potentials. The marginal of $x_n$ is a sum over $K^{n-1}$ configurations. Pushing each sum inside the product removes one variable at a time:
$$
\sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}} \prod_{t=1}^{n-1} \psi_t(x_t, x_{t+1}) = \sum_{x_{n-1}} \psi_{n-1}(x_{n-1}, x_n) \cdots \sum_{x_1} \psi_1(x_1, x_2),
$$
which costs $O(nK^2)$ operations instead of $O(K^n)$.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Factor graph]{.tag} A factor graph is a bipartite graph between variable nodes $i$ and factor nodes $f$, where $f$ is linked to the variables $x_f$ it depends on. It represents
$$
p(x) = \frac1Z \prod_f \psi_f(x_f).
$$
:::

Directed and undirected models both convert to factor graphs. On a general graph, the cost of elimination is exponential in the size of the largest clique created during elimination, which depends on the elimination order. The best order makes this size the treewidth plus one. Exact inference is NP-hard in general (Cooper, 1990).

### 5.2 Sum-product and max-product on trees

The **sum-product** algorithm sends messages along the edges of a factor graph. A variable sends to a factor the product of its other incoming messages. A factor sends to a variable the sum, over its other variables, of its potential times their incoming messages:
$$
m_{i \to f}(x_i) = \prod_{g \ni i,\, g \ne f} m_{g \to i}(x_i), \qquad m_{f \to i}(x_i) = \sum_{x_{f \setminus i}} \psi_f(x_f) \prod_{j \in f,\, j \ne i} m_{j \to f}(x_j).
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Sum-product is exact on trees]{.tag} If the factor graph is a tree, schedule messages from the leaves to a root, then back to the leaves; this uses two messages per edge. Then, for every variable:
$$
p(x_i) = \frac1Z \prod_{f \ni i} m_{f \to i}(x_i), \qquad Z = \sum_{x_i} \prod_{f \ni i} m_{f \to i}(x_i).
$$

::: proof
Removing the edge $(f, i)$ splits the tree in two. Let $T_{f \to i}$ be the part containing $f$. We show by induction on its size that $m_{f \to i}(x_i)$ is the sum, over the variables of $T_{f \to i}$ other than $x_i$, of the product of its factors.

-   For a leaf factor, this is the definition of the message.
-   In general, $T_{f \to i}$ is $f$ plus the disjoint subtrees hanging from its other variables $j$. These share no variable, so the sum of the product is a product of sums (the distributive law). Each sum is a message $m_{j \to f}$, by the induction hypothesis applied to the subtrees of $j$.

The factors around $x_i$ partition the whole tree, so the product of incoming messages is the unnormalised marginal of $x_i$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Replacing sums by maxima gives **max-product**. It computes max-marginals, and backtracking the argmaxes returns a most probable configuration (MAP). On graphs with cycles, the same updates define **loopy belief propagation**, which often works well but has no general guarantee (Murphy, Weiss and Jordan, 1999).

### 5.3 Hidden Markov models: forward–backward and Viterbi

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Hidden Markov model]{.tag} A hidden chain $z_1, \dots, z_T$ with $K$ states and observations $x_1, \dots, x_T$:
$$
p(x_{1:T}, z_{1:T}) = \pi_{z_1} \prod_{t=2}^T A_{z_{t-1} z_t} \prod_{t=1}^T b_{z_t}(x_t),
$$
with initial law $\pi$, transition matrix $A$ and emission densities $b_k$.
:::

The HMM factor graph is a chain, so sum-product applies. Its two passes are the **forward** and **backward** recursions, for $\alpha_t(k) = p(x_{1:t}, z_t = k)$ and $\beta_t(k) = p(x_{t+1:T} \mid z_t = k)$:
$$
\alpha_{t+1}(k) = b_k(x_{t+1}) \sum_j \alpha_t(j) A_{jk}, \qquad \beta_t(j) = \sum_k A_{jk}\, b_k(x_{t+1})\, \beta_{t+1}(k).
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Posterior marginals of an HMM]{.tag} The likelihood is $p(x_{1:T}) = \sum_k \alpha_T(k)$. The posteriors of one state and of two consecutive states are
$$
\gamma_t(k) = \frac{\alpha_t(k)\, \beta_t(k)}{p(x_{1:T})}, \qquad \xi_t(j, k) = \frac{\alpha_t(j)\, A_{jk}\, b_k(x_{t+1})\, \beta_{t+1}(k)}{p(x_{1:T})} .
$$

::: proof
Given $z_t$, the past $(x_{1:t})$ and the future $(x_{t+1:T})$ are independent: $z_t$ blocks every path of the chain (Theorem 4.4). So
$$
p(x_{1:T}, z_t = k) = p(x_{1:t}, z_t = k)\; p(x_{t+1:T} \mid z_t = k) = \alpha_t(k)\,\beta_t(k).
$$

The same argument at the pair $(z_t, z_{t+1})$ gives $\xi_t$. The recursions are sum-product messages on the chain, or follow directly by conditioning on the neighbouring state. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The cost is $O(TK^2)$. The $\alpha_t$ underflow for long sequences, so one normalises them at each step and keeps the normalisers $c_t$; then $\log p(x_{1:T}) = \sum_t \log c_t$. The **Viterbi** algorithm is max-product in the log domain. When the states and observations are Gaussian with linear dynamics, the same recursions become the Kalman filter and smoother.

```python
import itertools
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]])        # transitions  A[i, j] = p(z_t+1 = j | z_t = i)
B = np.array([[0.7, 0.2, 0.1], [0.1, 0.3, 0.6]])  # emissions  B[i, o] = p(x_t = o | z_t = i)
pi0 = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
x = [0, 0, 2, 2, 1, 2]
T, K = len(x), 2

alpha, c = np.zeros((T, K)), np.zeros(T)       # scaled forward pass
for t in range(T):
    a = pi0 * B[:, x[t]] if t == 0 else (alpha[t - 1] @ A) * B[:, x[t]]
    c[t] = a.sum(); alpha[t] = a / c[t]
beta = np.ones((T, K))                         # scaled backward pass
for t in range(T - 2, -1, -1):
    beta[t] = A @ (B[:, x[t + 1]] * beta[t + 1]) / c[t + 1]
gamma = alpha * beta                           # p(z_t | x_1:T)

# brute force over the K**T hidden paths
joint = {z: pi0[z[0]] * np.prod([A[z[t - 1], z[t]] for t in range(1, T)])
            * np.prod([B[z[t], x[t]] for t in range(T)])
         for z in itertools.product(range(K), repeat=T)}
px = sum(joint.values())
g_bf = np.array([[sum(p for z, p in joint.items() if z[t] == k) / px for k in range(K)] for t in range(T)])
print(f"log p(x): forward {np.log(c).sum():.6f}   brute force {np.log(px):.6f}")
print("max |gamma - brute force| =", np.abs(gamma - g_bf).max())

delta, back = np.log(pi0 * B[:, x[0]]), []    # Viterbi (max-product in logs)
for t in range(1, T):
    s = delta[:, None] + np.log(A)
    back.append(s.argmax(0)); delta = s.max(0) + np.log(B[:, x[t]])
path = [int(delta.argmax())]
for bp in reversed(back):
    path.append(int(bp[path[-1]]))
print("Viterbi path:", path[::-1], "  brute force:", list(max(joint, key=joint.get)))
```

The forward pass gives $\log p(x_{1:6}) = -6.651829$, equal to the sum over the $2^6 = 64$ hidden paths. The posteriors agree to $10^{-15}$, and Viterbi returns the path $(0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1)$ found by enumeration.

### 5.4 Learning an HMM: Baum–Welch

Baum–Welch is EM (ch. 2.2) for the HMM. The E-step computes $\gamma$ and $\xi$ by forward–backward. As for mixtures (Proposition 2.4), the M-step replaces counts of states and transitions by their expectations:
$$
\pi_k = \gamma_1(k), \qquad A_{jk} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \xi_t(j, k)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_t(j)}, \qquad b_k(o) = \frac{\sum_t \gamma_t(k)\, \mathbb 1[x_t = o]}{\sum_t \gamma_t(k)} .
$$

With Gaussian emissions, the last update becomes a $\gamma$-weighted mean and covariance. By Theorem 2.3, each iteration does not decrease the likelihood. As for mixtures, the result depends on the initialisation, and several restarts are standard.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Exact inference is the distributive law: push sums inside products.
-   On a tree factor graph, two passes of sum-product give all marginals and $Z$; max-product gives the MAP.
-   Forward–backward and Viterbi are sum-product and max-product on the HMM chain, at cost $O(TK^2)$.
-   Baum–Welch is EM with expected transition and emission counts.
:::

## 6. Approximate inference I: Monte Carlo and MCMC {#ch6}

When the graph has cycles or the variables are continuous and non-Gaussian, exact sums are out of reach. Monte Carlo methods replace them by averages over samples. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) produces such samples from a density known only up to its normalising constant, which is exactly what posteriors and Gibbs distributions provide.

### 6.1 Monte Carlo and importance sampling

For $x_1, \dots, x_n$ i.i.d. from $p$, the average of $f(x_i)$ is unbiased for $\mathbb E_p[f]$, with variance $\mathrm{Var}_p(f)/n$, whatever the dimension.

When the target is hard to sample, draw from a proposal $q$ and reweight.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.1 — Importance sampling]{.tag} If $q > 0$ wherever $p > 0$, then, for every $p$-integrable $f$,
$$
\mathbb E_p[f(X)] = \mathbb E_q\big[f(X)\, w(X)\big], \qquad w = \frac{p}{q} .
$$

If $p = \tilde p / Z$ is known only up to $Z$, the **self-normalised** estimator with $w_i = \tilde p(x_i) / q(x_i)$ is consistent:
$$
\hat I_n = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, f(x_i)}{\sum_i w_i} .
$$

::: proof
The first identity is $\int f\, \frac{p}{q}\, q = \int f p$.

For the second, the numerator and the denominator, divided by $n$, converge almost surely to $Z\, \mathbb E_p[f]$ and $Z$, by the law of large numbers. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The quality of the weights is summarised by the **effective sample size** $(\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$. In high dimension, the weights of a fixed proposal degenerate: a few samples carry all the mass. Importance sampling returns in ch. 8.3, inside the IWAE bound.

### 6.2 Metropolis–Hastings

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — Metropolis–Hastings algorithm]{.tag} Target $\pi \propto \tilde\pi$, proposal kernel $q(y \mid x)$. From the current state $x$:

1.  draw $y \sim q(\cdot \mid x)$;
2.  accept $y$ with probability
    $$
    a(x, y) = \min\Big(1,\; \frac{\tilde\pi(y)\, q(x \mid y)}{\tilde\pi(x)\, q(y \mid x)}\Big);
    $$
3.  otherwise stay at $x$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Metropolis–Hastings leaves the target invariant]{.tag} The Metropolis–Hastings kernel $P$ satisfies detailed balance with respect to $\pi$, hence
$$
\pi P = \pi .
$$

::: proof
For $y \ne x$, the transition density is $P(x, y) = q(y \mid x)\, a(x, y)$. Then
$$
\pi(x)\, q(y \mid x)\, a(x, y) = \min\big(\pi(x) q(y \mid x),\; \pi(y) q(x \mid y)\big),
$$
which is symmetric in $(x, y)$. So $\pi(x) P(x, y) = \pi(y) P(y, x)$; the rejection mass at $x$ satisfies this trivially.

Integrating detailed balance over $x$ gives $\int \pi(x) P(x, y)\, dx = \pi(y)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Invariance is not convergence. If the chain is also irreducible and aperiodic, the law of $x_t$ converges to $\pi$, and ergodic averages satisfy a law of large numbers (Robert and Casella, 2004). For a random-walk proposal in high dimension, a classical result recommends tuning the step to an acceptance rate near 0.234 (Roberts, Gelman and Gilks, 1997).

### 6.3 Gibbs sampling

The Gibbs sampler updates one variable at a time from its full conditional $p(x_i \mid x_{-i})$, cycling over $i$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — Gibbs is Metropolis–Hastings with acceptance one]{.tag} The Gibbs update of coordinate $i$ is a Metropolis–Hastings step with proposal $q(y \mid x) = p(y_i \mid x_{-i})$ for $y_{-i} = x_{-i}$, and its acceptance probability is $1$.

::: proof
With $y_{-i} = x_{-i}$, the factorisation $p(x) = p(x_{-i})\, p(x_i \mid x_{-i})$ gives
$$
\frac{p(y)\, q(x \mid y)}{p(x)\, q(y \mid x)} = \frac{p(x_{-i})\, p(y_i \mid x_{-i})\, p(x_i \mid x_{-i})}{p(x_{-i})\, p(x_i \mid x_{-i})\, p(y_i \mid x_{-i})} = 1.
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In a graphical model, the full conditional depends only on the **Markov blanket**: the neighbours in an undirected graph, or the parents, children and co-parents in a DAG. For the Ising model of ch. 4.4, with $\sigma$ the logistic function:
$$
p(x_i = +1 \mid x_{-i}) = \sigma\Big(2\big(h_i + \textstyle\sum_{j} J_{ij} x_j\big)\Big).
$$

Gibbs mixes slowly when variables are strongly coupled: in a highly correlated Gaussian, coordinate moves are tiny. Blocking correlated variables or reparameterising helps.

### 6.4 Langevin dynamics

Write the target as $\pi \propto e^{-U}$. The **overdamped Langevin diffusion** follows the gradient of $\log \pi$ plus noise:
$$
dX_t = -\nabla U(X_t)\, dt + \sqrt 2\, dW_t .
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.5 — The Langevin diffusion leaves $\pi$ invariant]{.tag} The law $\rho_t$ of $X_t$ solves the Fokker–Planck equation, and $\pi$ is one of its stationary solutions:
$$
\partial_t \rho = \nabla \cdot (\rho\, \nabla U) + \Delta \rho = \nabla \cdot \big(\rho\, \nabla U + \nabla \rho\big).
$$

::: proof
For $\rho = \pi = e^{-U}/Z$, we have $\nabla \pi = -\pi \nabla U$. So the flux $\pi \nabla U + \nabla \pi$ is zero, and $\partial_t \pi = 0$. Under growth conditions on $U$, $\rho_t \to \pi$ (Roberts and Tweedie, 1996). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Euler discretisation with step $h$ is the **unadjusted Langevin algorithm** (ULA):
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - h\, \nabla U(x_k) + \sqrt{2h}\; \xi_k, \qquad \xi_k \sim \mathcal N(0, I).
$$

ULA is biased: its stationary law differs from $\pi$ by an amount controlled by $h$ (Durmus and Moulines, 2017). Using the ULA move as the proposal of a Metropolis–Hastings step removes the bias: this is **MALA**.

::: ex
[Example 6.6 — The bias of ULA, computed]{.tag} For $\pi = \mathcal N(0, 1)$, $U(x) = x^2/2$ and ULA reads $x_{k+1} = (1 - h)\,x_k + \sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k$. A stationary variance $v$ must satisfy $v = (1 - h)^2 v + 2h$, hence
$$
v = \frac{1}{1 - h/2} .
$$

For $h = 0.5$, this gives $v = 4/3 \approx 1.333$ instead of $1$.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
U = lambda x: 0.5 * x ** 2            # target pi = N(0, 1), potential U = -log pi
gradU = lambda x: x

def run(h, n=200_000, adjust=False):
    x, xs, acc = 0.0, np.empty(n), 0
    for i in range(n):
        y = x - h * gradU(x) + np.sqrt(2 * h) * rng.normal()      # Langevin proposal
        if adjust:                                                 # MALA: MH correction
            logq = lambda a, b: -(a - b + h * gradU(b)) ** 2 / (4 * h)
            if np.log(rng.random()) < U(x) - U(y) + logq(x, y) - logq(y, x):
                x, acc = y, acc + 1
        else:
            x = y                                                  # ULA: always accept
        xs[i] = x
    return xs.var(), acc / n

for h in [0.1, 0.5]:
    v_ula, _ = run(h)
    v_mala, a = run(h, adjust=True)
    print(f"h = {h}: ULA variance {v_ula:.3f} (theory {1 / (1 - h / 2):.3f})"
          f" | MALA variance {v_mala:.3f}, acceptance {a:.2f}")
```

With $h = 0.5$, ULA's empirical variance is 1.338, as Example 6.6 predicts, while MALA gives 0.995 with 92 % acceptance. Langevin dynamics need only the gradient of $\log \pi$, the **score**. Score-based diffusion models (ch. 10.3) run it with a learned score.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Importance sampling reweights samples from a proposal; its weights degenerate in high dimension.
-   Metropolis–Hastings satisfies detailed balance for any proposal and needs $\pi$ only up to a constant.
-   Gibbs sampling is Metropolis–Hastings with full conditionals, which depend only on the Markov blanket.
-   Langevin dynamics follow the score; discretised, they are biased (ULA) unless corrected (MALA).
:::

## 7. Approximate inference II: variational methods, stochastic block models and expectation propagation {#ch7}

Variational methods turn inference into optimisation: choose, in a tractable family, the distribution closest to the posterior. They are deterministic and fast, and they plug directly into EM. This chapter covers mean field, variational EM, its application to stochastic block models for networks, and expectation propagation, which minimises the KL divergence in the other direction.

### 7.1 Variational inference and mean field

By Proposition 2.2, maximising the ELBO $\mathcal L(q)$ over a family $\mathcal Q$ is minimising $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p(z \mid x))$ over $\mathcal Q$. The **mean-field** family makes the latent coordinates independent:
$$
q(z) = \prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j).
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.1 — Coordinate ascent variational inference (CAVI)]{.tag} With all factors but $q_j$ fixed, the ELBO is maximised by
$$
q_j^\star(z_j) \;\propto\; \exp\Big(\mathbb E_{q_{-j}}\big[\log p(x, z)\big]\Big),
$$
where the expectation is over all coordinates except $z_j$.

::: proof
Let $\tilde q_j$ be the right-hand side, normalised. Isolating $q_j$ in the ELBO gives
$$
\mathcal L(q) = \mathbb E_{q_j}\Big[\mathbb E_{q_{-j}}[\log p(x, z)]\Big] - \mathbb E_{q_j}[\log q_j] + \text{const} = -\mathrm{KL}(q_j \,\|\, \tilde q_j) + \text{const}.
$$

This is maximal at $q_j = \tilde q_j$, by Gibbs' inequality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Cycling over $j$ never decreases the ELBO. It converges to a stationary point, in practice a local optimum, so the result depends on the initialisation.

Because $\mathrm{KL}(q \| p)$ penalises mass of $q$ where $p$ is small, the solution is **mode-seeking**: mean field underestimates posterior variances. For a Gaussian target with precision $\Lambda$, the optimal factor $q_j$ has variance $1/\Lambda_{jj}$, never larger than the true marginal variance (Exercise 11).

### 7.2 Variational EM

When the E-step of EM is intractable, restrict $q$ to $\mathcal Q$ and alternate:

1.  **VE-step**: maximise $\mathcal L(\cdot, \theta_t)$ over $q \in \mathcal Q$, for example by CAVI, giving $q_{t+1}$;
2.  **M-step**: maximise $\mathcal L(q_{t+1}, \cdot)$ over $\theta$, giving $\theta_{t+1}$.

By Proposition 3.5, this is coordinate ascent on the free energy over a smaller set. The ELBO increases at each step. The likelihood itself need not increase, because the gap $\mathrm{KL}(q \| p(z \mid x; \theta))$ no longer vanishes.

### 7.3 Stochastic block models

::: def
[Definition 7.2 — Stochastic block model (SBM)]{.tag} Each of $n$ nodes has a latent class $z_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}$, drawn i.i.d. with $p(z_i = k) = \alpha_k$. Given the classes, the edges $X_{ij}$, $i < j$, are independent:
$$
X_{ij} \mid z_i = k,\, z_j = l \;\sim\; \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{kl}).
$$

The model was introduced by Holland, Laskey and Leinhardt (1983); its estimation by Nowicki and Snijders (2001).
:::

Diagonal-dominant $\pi$ gives communities, but the model also captures hubs, bipartite and core–periphery structures. Exact EM fails: every edge $X_{ij}$ is a common child of $z_i$ and $z_j$, so moralisation couples all the labels. The posterior $p(z \mid X)$ does not factorise, and its normaliser sums over $K^n$ labellings.

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — Variational EM for the SBM (Daudin, Picard and Robin, 2008)]{.tag} Take the mean-field family $q(z) = \prod_i \mathrm{Cat}(z_i; \tau_i)$. The VE-step solves the fixed-point equations
$$
\tau_{ik} \;\propto\; \alpha_k \prod_{j \ne i} \prod_{l} \Big[\pi_{kl}^{X_{ij}} (1 - \pi_{kl})^{1 - X_{ij}}\Big]^{\tau_{jl}} .
$$

The M-step is
$$
\alpha_k = \frac1n \sum_i \tau_{ik}, \qquad \pi_{kl} = \frac{\sum_{i \ne j} \tau_{ik}\, \tau_{jl}\, X_{ij}}{\sum_{i \ne j} \tau_{ik}\, \tau_{jl}} .
$$

::: proof
The complete log-likelihood is
$$
\log p(X, z) = \sum_{i,k} z_{ik} \log \alpha_k + \sum_{i < j} \sum_{k,l} z_{ik} z_{jl} \big[X_{ij} \log \pi_{kl} + (1 - X_{ij}) \log(1 - \pi_{kl})\big],
$$
with $z_{ik} = \mathbb 1[z_i = k]$.

Proposition 7.1 takes the expectation over $z_{-i}$, replacing each $z_{jl}$ by $\tau_{jl}$, which gives the VE-step.

The M-step maximises the same expression with $z_{ik} z_{jl}$ replaced by $\tau_{ik} \tau_{jl}$: weighted multinomial and Bernoulli likelihoods. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The number of classes is chosen by the **integrated classification likelihood** (ICL). For an undirected graph, Daudin et al. (2008) penalise the complete-data log-likelihood, evaluated at the estimated labels, by
$$
\frac{K - 1}{2} \log n + \frac{K(K+1)}{4} \log \frac{n(n-1)}{2} .
$$

The first term counts the $K - 1$ free proportions; the second counts the $K(K+1)/2$ connection probabilities, estimated from $n(n-1)/2$ pairs.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score as ari

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
n, K = 300, 3
z = rng.choice(K, n, p=[0.5, 0.3, 0.2])
P = np.full((K, K), 0.04) + 0.10 * np.eye(K)                 # assortative SBM
A = np.triu(rng.random((n, n)) < P[z][:, z], 1).astype(float)
A = A + A.T                                                   # undirected, no self-loop

U = np.linalg.eigh(A)[1][:, -K:]                              # spectral initialisation
z0 = KMeans(K, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(U)
tau = np.eye(K)[z0] * 0.9 + 0.1 / K
off = 1 - A - np.eye(n)                                       # non-edges, j != i
for it in range(50):
    alpha = tau.mean(0)                                       # M-step
    Pi = (tau.T @ A @ tau) / (tau.T @ (1 - np.eye(n)) @ tau)
    Pi = Pi.clip(1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
    for _ in range(5):                                        # E-step: fixed point on tau
        S = np.log(alpha) + A @ tau @ np.log(Pi).T + off @ tau @ np.log(1 - Pi).T
        tau = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True))
        tau /= tau.sum(1, keepdims=True)

print("ARI spectral init:", round(ari(z, z0), 3))
print("ARI after VEM:    ", round(ari(z, tau.argmax(1)), 3))
print("estimated alpha", np.round(np.sort(alpha), 2), "\nestimated Pi\n", np.round(Pi, 3))
```

Spectral clustering of the adjacency matrix gives an adjusted Rand index of 0.86. Variational EM, started from it, reaches 0.975, and recovers the proportions $(0.23, 0.29, 0.48)$ and connection probabilities within 0.005 of the truth (0.14 inside, 0.04 between).

### 7.4 Expectation propagation

Expectation propagation (EP; Minka, 2001) targets posteriors of the form
$$
p(\theta \mid \mathcal D) \;\propto\; p_0(\theta) \prod_{i=1}^n t_i(\theta),
$$
and approximates each **site** $t_i$ by a member $\tilde t_i$ of an exponential family. Its building block is a KL projection in the direction opposite to variational inference.

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.4 — Projection by moment matching]{.tag} Let $\mathcal F$ be an exponential family with sufficient statistic $T$ (Definition 0.5). If the minimiser
$$
q^\star = \arg\min_{q \in \mathcal F} \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)
$$
exists, it matches the expected sufficient statistics:
$$
\mathbb E_{q^\star}[T(X)] = \mathbb E_p[T(X)].
$$

::: proof
For $q_\eta \in \mathcal F$, expanding the logarithm gives, with $c$ independent of $\eta$:
$$
\mathrm{KL}(p \| q_\eta) = -\eta^\top \mathbb E_p[T] + A(\eta) + c .
$$

This is convex in $\eta$, and by Proposition 0.6 its gradient is $\mathbb E_{q_\eta}[T] - \mathbb E_p[T]$. It vanishes at the minimiser. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a Gaussian family, $q^\star$ matches the mean and the covariance of $p$. EP iterates over the sites:

1.  **cavity**: remove site $i$, giving $q^{\setminus i} \propto q / \tilde t_i$;
2.  **tilted distribution**: put back the exact site, giving $\hat p_i \propto q^{\setminus i}\, t_i$;
3.  **projection**: set $q_{\text{new}}$ to the moment-matched projection of $\hat p_i$ onto $\mathcal F$ (Proposition 7.4);
4.  **site update**: $\tilde t_i \propto q_{\text{new}} / q^{\setminus i}$.

Each step needs only one-dimensional or low-dimensional integrals against one exact site, which are often available in closed form, as for probit likelihoods. A single pass is *assumed density filtering*. EP has no general convergence guarantee. Where it converges, it tends to cover the posterior mass better than mean field, which is why it is a standard choice for Gaussian-process classification (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006, chapter 3).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   Variational inference maximises the ELBO over a tractable family; CAVI updates each factor to the exponential of an expected log-joint.
-   Mean field is mode-seeking and underestimates variances.
-   Variational EM increases the ELBO, not necessarily the likelihood.
-   SBM labels are coupled by every edge; mean-field VEM and ICL make the model usable on networks.
-   EP projects local tilted distributions by moment matching, minimising KL in the other direction.
:::

## 8. Deep latent variable models, variational auto-encoders and amortised inference {#ch8}

Replace the linear map of probabilistic PCA (ch. 2.4) by a neural network, and the model can generate images, sounds or molecules. The price is that neither the likelihood nor the posterior has a closed form any more. This chapter combines the ELBO of ch. 2, an inference network shared by all data points, and a gradient estimator that goes through sampling.

### 8.1 Deep latent variable models

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Deep latent variable model (DLVM)]{.tag} A prior $p(z) = \mathcal N(0, I_q)$ and an observation model whose parameters are the output of a neural network $f_\theta$, the **decoder**: for example $x \mid z \sim \mathcal N(f_\theta(z), \sigma^2 I)$ for real data, or independent Bernoulli pixels with logits $f_\theta(z)$. The likelihood is
$$
p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz .
$$
:::

The integral has no closed form, and neither does the posterior $p_\theta(z \mid x)$, so the E-step of EM is impossible. A further subtlety: with a Gaussian decoder whose variance is also learned, the likelihood of a DLVM can be unbounded, like that of a Gaussian mixture (ch. 2.1). Mattei and Frellsen (2018) analyse this degeneracy.

### 8.2 Amortised variational inference and the VAE

Variational EM would optimise one distribution $q_i(z)$ per data point. **Amortised** inference replaces them by a single network, the **encoder**, that maps $x$ to the parameters of $q_\phi(z \mid x)$, typically a Gaussian with mean $\mu_\phi(x)$ and diagonal variances $\sigma^2_\phi(x)$. The **variational auto-encoder** (VAE; Kingma and Welling, 2014; Rezende, Mohamed and Wierstra, 2014) maximises over $(\theta, \phi)$ the sum over data points of

::: key
[Key result — the VAE objective]{.tag}
$$
\mathcal L(\theta, \phi; x) = \mathbb E_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\big) \;\le\; \log p_\theta(x).
$$
:::

The first term is a reconstruction error; the second keeps the codes close to the prior. For a diagonal Gaussian $q$ and a standard normal prior, the KL term is explicit:
$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal N(\mu, \mathrm{diag}\,\sigma^2) \,\|\, \mathcal N(0, I)\big) = \frac12 \sum_{j=1}^q \big(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2\big).
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.2 — The reparameterisation trick]{.tag} Write $z$ as a differentiable function of $\phi$ and of a noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$ whose law does not depend on $\phi$:
$$
z = g_\phi(\varepsilon, x) = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon .
$$

For a differentiable $h$, under domination conditions:
$$
\nabla_\phi\, \mathbb E_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[h(z)\big] = \mathbb E_{\varepsilon}\big[\nabla_\phi\, h(g_\phi(\varepsilon, x))\big].
$$

::: proof
